title: Why reflect on death
hook: everyone knows the battery runs out; the Buddha says remembering death leads to the deathless
tomorrow: one more day to practice, or one more breath: which did he praise?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the householder's path closed at a sickbed: Nakula's mother, steady, answering every worry. Practice is everywhere. Today a new stretch opens, on death and dying, gently.
screen: `PRACTICE IS EVERYWHERE.` → `A NEW STRETCH: DEATH AND DYING.`

segments.voice: Everyone knows they'll die, the way everyone knows a phone battery runs out: in theory, and never while it's at eighty percent. So why think about it on purpose? The Buddha's answer comes with a strange twist. He says that remembering death, practiced well, plunges into the deathless and ends in the deathless. Thinking about death leads to no-death? That's today's puzzle.
screen: `THE BATTERY AT EIGHTY PERCENT.` → `WHY THINK ABOUT IT ON PURPOSE?` → `DEATH LEADS TO THE DEATHLESS?`

segments.voice: The line opens a sutta in the Anguttara Nikaya. Mindfulness of death, developed and practiced often, the Buddha says, brings great fruit and great benefit; it plunges into the deathless. The Pali for deathless is amata, and here it doesn't mean living forever in this body. It's a name for nibbana, the peace the Buddha taught as beyond birth and death. So how does remembering death point there? Start with the eighty-percent feeling. While the battery seems full, everything can wait: the apology, the practice, the call to a grandparent. Remembering death drains that fake charge. Priorities sort themselves. A grudge looks small. Kindness looks urgent. And underneath, something loosens: the grip on things that were never going to stay. That loosening, letting go, is the road the Buddha says leads to the deathless. This isn't one school's habit. In the Theravada world, the Visuddhimagga, a classic meditation manual, gives mindfulness of death a long section of its own. In Tibet, it's the opening of the path, through a teaching handed down from Atisha that the next days will open. In Zen halls, a wooden board struck before sitting often carries a verse: birth and death are a great matter; impermanence is swift. Different schools, one move. The aim isn't fear. It's waking up while the battery still has charge, to live well.
screen: `IT PLUNGES INTO THE DEATHLESS.` · `AMATA: A NAME FOR NIBBANA.` · `THE FAKE CHARGE DRAINS.` · `THERAVADA, TIBET, ZEN.` · then, large: `TO LIVE WELL.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes or lower them, and let one quiet sentence rest in the mind: this life will end, and today is part of it. If fear comes, let it be there, and come back to the breath. If thoughts of death feel heavy or unsafe for you right now, skip this and reach out to someone; in the US you can call or text 988.
Why reflect on death: because remembering it drains the fake charge, loosens the grip, and turns a life toward what matters.
For the road: remember death, to live well, while the battery still has charge. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1626 COUNTS.` → `DEATH AND DYING · 1 OF 30.` → `TOMORROW: ONE MORE DAY, OR ONE MORE BREATH?`

howItsDone: Reflection on death is taught across Buddhist schools: as one of the recollections in Theravada meditation, as the opening contemplation of the Tibetan lamrim, and in Zen through verses on birth and death; teachers usually pair it with calm and kindness rather than fear.

fork.setup: your friend keeps putting off calling her grandfather: 'there's always next weekend.' which reading of today's sutta fits?
options: remembering death drains the 'always next weekend' feeling, so the call matters now.
thinking about death is morbid; better to keep things light with her.
the deathless means there's no rush; everything continues anyway.
fork.reveal: the eighty-percent feeling lets everything wait. remembering death sorts priorities and turns a life toward what matters.

original.note: Pali: maranassati, mindfulness of death, from marana (death) and sati (mindfulness).

trapdoor: what you thought: thinking about death is a downer.
what it means: remembering death drains the false sense of endless time, loosens clinging and points toward the deathless.
what a scholar hears: AN 6.19 opens by calling mindfulness of death of great fruit, plunging into and ending in the deathless (amata), a name for nibbana.
guess: remembering death so you live with clear priorities
a ritual for calling back the spirits of the dead
a way of making peace with fear by avoiding it

chat.says: after we saw bác Hùng, ông said in the car, 'good practice for me too.' kind of morbid??
options: Not morbid. Remembering death is meant to wake him up to living well.
A bit. Buddhists think about death because life is mostly sad.
He's being polite. Nobody really reflects on death on purpose.
chat.meaning: The Buddha calls mindfulness of death of great benefit: it drains the fake 'always later' and turns a life toward what matters.

tie.story: The Buddha said remembering death, practiced well, plunges into the deathless.

amata.meaning: the deathless; in the suttas, a name for nibbana

nibbana.meaning: the peace beyond craving, birth and death (Sanskrit nirvana)

Visuddhimagga.meaning: the Path of Purification, a classic Theravada meditation manual

Atisha.meaning: an Indian Buddhist teacher whose teachings shaped Tibetan practice

Theravada.meaning: the school of the elders, found in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia
